clinicalPearls: Constipation is defined by symptoms including infrequent stools, straining, hard stools, and a sense of incomplete evacuation rather than by stool frequency alone
Most chronic constipation is functional and can be categorised as normal-transit, slow-transit, or a defecatory (pelvic floor) disorder
A careful history and rectal examination are essential and can reveal a defecatory disorder such as dyssynergic defaecation
Secondary causes including hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes, neurological disease, and constipating medications should be identified and treated
Increasing dietary fibre and fluid with graded use of osmotic and stimulant laxatives is the mainstay for most patients
Defecatory disorders respond poorly to laxatives alone and are best treated with biofeedback-directed pelvic floor retraining
Anorectal manometry with a balloon expulsion test and, where needed, transit studies guide management of refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic constipation reflects disordered colonic transit, defecatory mechanics, or both. In slow-transit constipation, reduced colonic propulsive activity, often linked to abnormalities of enteric neurons and interstitial cells of Cajal, delays stool passage. In defecatory disorders, impaired coordination of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter (dyssynergia) or structural pelvic floor abnormalities prevent effective evacuation. Normal-transit constipation, the most common type, involves normal stool movement with perceived difficulty, often overlapping with irritable bowel syndrome. Secondary causes act through metabolic, endocrine, neurological, or pharmacological effects on gut motility.
additionalDifferentials: Neurological disease such as Parkinson disease or spinal cord lesions
Medication effects (opioids, anticholinergics, calcium and iron supplements)
Pelvic floor dyssynergia or rectal prolapse
additionalInvestigations: Digital rectal examination to assess sphincter tone and defecatory function
Blood tests including thyroid function, calcium, glucose, and electrolytes
Colonoscopy when alarm features or age-appropriate screening indications are present
Colonic transit study for suspected slow transit
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion test for suspected defecatory disorder
redFlags: New or progressive constipation in an older patient
Family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease
Features of obstruction such as severe pain, distension, and vomiting
reference.prognosis: Chronic constipation is generally benign but frequently persistent and can significantly reduce quality of life; most patients improve with lifestyle measures and laxatives, and biofeedback is effective for defecatory disorders, though a minority remain refractory.
pitfalls: Escalating laxatives without recognising an underlying defecatory disorder that needs biofeedback
Failing to exclude secondary and structural causes before treating symptomatically
Omitting the rectal examination, which often reveals the mechanism of constipation
management: First-line lifestyle measures with increased dietary fibre, adequate fluid intake and physical activity
Graded use of osmotic laxatives such as macrogol, adding stimulant laxatives when fibre and osmotic agents are insufficient
Secretagogues and prokinetics such as prucalopride, linaclotide or lubiprostone for refractory or slow-transit constipation
Biofeedback-directed pelvic floor retraining for defecatory dyssynergic disorders, which respond poorly to laxatives alone
Identification and treatment of secondary causes including hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes and neurological disease, with review and withdrawal of constipating medications
Colonoscopy where alarm features or age-appropriate screening indications are present
Specialist referral for anorectal manometry and transit studies, reserving surgery for carefully selected refractory slow-transit cases
